newsitem.title: FRANCE: Right leads a week ahead of French election.
newsitem.headline: Right leads a week ahead of French election.

text.p: The campaign for France's snap parliamentary election entered its last week on Saturday with the left gnawing at the ruling centre-right's lead.

The latest opinion polls saw the margin in favour of Prime Minister Alain Juppe's conservatives being slightly eroded with seven days to go before campaigning for the May 25 first round ends next Friday night.

A BVA survey of mainland France's 555 constituencies said Juppe's coalition would win a 50-seat majority over the combined left, down from 52 a week earlier. Most of the 22 other overseas constituencies are held by the goverment.
The poll showed the centre-right with 302 seats to 228 for the Socialists, two for their ecologist allies, 22 for the Communists and one for the National Front.
Another survey, by CSA, said the centre-right coalition would win 299 seats to the combined left's 256 -- a majority of 43 seats, well down on CSA's week-earlier forecast of a 80-seat margin.
Another burst of opinion polls was expected later in the day before a ban on them in the week before voting takes effect at midnight (2200 GMT).
The ban means no more election polls will be published before the election is over since the second round of voting, on June 1, takes place a week after the first.
"There will be no more polls from Sunday, and voters will thus have to make their decision in democratic meditation," said Socialist Party leader Lionel Jospin.

As surveys indicated that 23 to 38 percent of voters were still undecided, unconfirmed reports said Gaullist President Jacques Chirac could intervene on behalf of the conservatives after returning from a state visit to China on Sunday.

Jospin said a second intervention into the campaign by Chirac, who earlier this month published a newspaper column to back the conservatives, would "distort democracy" and he would demand the right to respond.

Alarmed by reports that many conservative voters could stay away from the first round or cast blank ballots to mark their discontent over economic policies and political corruption, Juppe has warned that protest votes or abstention would favour the left and could return the Socialists after they were routed in 1993.
Foreign policy briefly burst into a campaign dominated by domestic issues on Saturday as Jospin branded the downfall of Mobutu Sese Seko a setback for the government.

"What is happening in Zaire certainly seals in a way the failure of France's African policy," he said. "The current government was wrong to put president Mobutu back in the saddle after we had tried to sideline him," he told reporters.
France clung to Mobutu long after other western powers had dropped him and was pushed to the diplomatic sidelines as Laurent Kabila's rebels inexorably advanced towards power.

There was no indication whether Mobutu could choose exile in France, where he owns a luxury Riviera mansion. Analysts said Paris was unlikely to offer him shelter until after the election for fear that his presence could become a campaign issue.
Former Socialist Party chief Henri Emmanuelli seized on the sale of 30 Airbus airliners to China during Chirac's state visit to snipe at the conservatives' privatisation policies.

He told a rally that bickering conservative leaders agreed on one thing: privatisation. "And what does Jacques (Chirac) sell in China? Private sector products? Not at all. Airbus planes, the jewel of Aerospatiale, a state company," he said.
